data.content_ref: inline:The target answers the cross-city variation half of the question (sky view factor scaling with building height/density) but misattributes the primary cause of the baseline nocturnal UHI gap itself. It frames the warmer city as mainly a 'radiative-geometry effect' of reduced sky view trapping longwave radiation. But the dominant nocturnal UHI mechanism is the slow release of stored daytime heat by high thermal-mass urban materials; street-canyon geometry and reduced sky view is a secondary or modifying factor. By demoting thermal mass to a 'secondary role' and making reduced radiative cooling the primary explanation, the answer gives a less accurate single-mechanism account of why the city is several degrees warmer at night. The cross-city modulator it identifies (building height/density) actually affects nocturnal UHI largely because taller, denser canyons also enclose more thermally massive fabric and reduce ventilation, not because longwave trapping alone dominates.
